audience.description: Reader has read Part I; undergraduate calculus/basic probability/linear algebra and expected value, variance, SD and density are assumed. Earlier 01-foundations teaches neural spikes/recurrent feedback, 01b-persistence teaches fixed points/continuous attractors/neutral directions, and 02-memory-dynamics teaches Brownian increments and diffusion. These earlier concepts are not silently assumed electronics knowledge. The Part opening assumes calculus, basic probability and linear algebra. Chapters07/08 teach electronics, weight/state/readout separation, feedback and error types. No unmentioned electronics or machine-learning background is assumed. Undergraduate calculus, basic probability and linear algebra; expected value, variance, standard deviation and density are known. Earlier Part I teaches Brownian increments, local diffusion, stochastic conventions and neutral projection. These subject-specific prerequisites were read in actual source and are not treated as audience assumptions.

aliases: connection setting versus changing state versus remembered value

sections.heading: A connection setting shapes activity. The activity can represent a cue
Bits, capacitor voltages, and material conductances store different physical states
The stored state matters through the update it produces
Feedback can extend persistence beyond a component's decay time
A bit corrects small displacements. A continuous memory preserves some of them
Silicon experiments distinguish discrete persistence from graded representation
Digital and analog implementations expose different parts of the neural model
Recent results improve temporal computation, adaptation, and device stability
Explicit slow memory is a current design choice, with distinct costs
Repeated cue-and-delay trials separate drift from random spreading
Physical parameters act through decay, bias, and noise projection
Matching time and readout is necessary to compare memory accuracy

passages.text: A silicon circuit can keep a connection strength unchanged while losing the angle it was asked to remember. It can also keep that angle while its individual electrical signals change. To compare electronic memory with the neural memory in Part I, we first need to identify what information each physical quantity represents. This chapter separates the connection settings, the changing state of each artificial neuron, and the value represented by their joint activity. That separation will let us ask what feedback actually preserves.

Imagine giving a circuit a brief cue for an angle of $30^\circ$. After the cue ends, a connected group of artificial neurons remains active. We estimate the remembered angle from which neurons are active and how strongly. The experiment involves:
**Connection weights** determine how a signal from one neuron changes another neuron's state. A weight can be fixed throughout the trial.
**Neuron and synapse states** change during the trial. Examples include a voltage, a current left by recent inputs, or a number representing either quantity.
**The remembered angle** is a property of the joint state, recovered by a readout rule. It need not occupy one dedicated storage cell.

[Keeping the weights unchanged preserves the circuit's rule of operation. Keeping the cue available requires the resulting activity to preserve information about that cue.]{.key-statement} Training can change the first object. Remembering a new angle can change the second and third without any further training.

[[**Neuromorphic computing**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} implements computations inspired by neural circuits using electronic systems organized around neurons, connections, events, or their dynamics.]{.definition-explanation} Some systems calculate neural states as digital numbers. Others use voltages and currents that evolve physically. A system can combine both approaches. The word alone does not tell us where its memory is stored or whether it demonstrates a biological memory mechanism.

[[**Working memory**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, in this Part, means keeping information about a recent input available for a later task.]{.definition-explanation} Persistent activity is one candidate mechanism. A slowly decaying state, a sequence of states, or an explicit digital buffer can also store recent information. We must specify the allowed delay and readout error before calling one implementation adequate.
<div class="publisher-worked-calculation publisher-fold-always">
**Example: the same weights can hold different angles.**

Suppose a ring of 32 artificial neurons has fixed local excitation and broader inhibition. A cue near neuron 3 creates a localized group of active neurons there. A later trial cues neuron 11 and creates a group near that location. The same connection weights support both trials. A decoder assigns an angle to the active group's center. If the group moves after the cue, the decoded angle changes even though every stored weight remains correct. This is an example constructed to illustrate the distinction. It is not a specification of a chip.

The neural model still needs a physical implementation. If the model has a variable called membrane voltage, a chip may store it as a binary number or as an actual circuit voltage. Those choices expose the computation to different errors. [[**Current**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is electric charge flowing per unit time, measured in amperes (coulombs per second).]{.definition-explanation} [[**Voltage**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is an electrical energy difference per unit charge, measured in volts (joules per coulomb).]{.definition-explanation}

A [[**capacitor**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} stores separated electric charge. For fixed capacitance $C$, its stored charge $Q$ and voltage difference $V$ satisfy $Q=CV$.]{.definition-explanation} Charge is measured in coulombs and capacitance in farads (coulombs per volt). Supplying current changes $Q$, so it changes the stored voltage.

<!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = NO --> [[**Digital storage**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} uses distinguishable physical ranges to represent discrete symbols, usually bits.]{.definition-explanation} In [[**static random-access memory (SRAM)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, powered transistor feedback maintains one of two states representing a bit.]{.definition-explanation} Several bits can encode a weight or a changing neuron variable. Reliable bits do not imply unlimited numerical precision: a finite word represents only finitely many values. <!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = YES -->

[[**Analog state**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} represents a model quantity through the magnitude of a physical variable, such as capacitor voltage.]{.definition-explanation} Input current changes stored charge and so changes voltage. Leakage changes that voltage during a quiet interval. Feedback or new input can oppose the leakage. In BrainScaleS-2, the membrane state evolves this way, while local SRAM stores the synaptic weights.[^hardware-pehle]

[[**Phase-change memory (PCM)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} stores information in a material's atomic arrangement, including the proportions of ordered and disordered regions, which affect its electrical resistance.]{.definition-explanation} Programming pulses heat the material. Its heating and cooling history changes the arrangement. [[**Conductance**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} measures the current produced per unit applied voltage where current is approximately proportional to voltage. It is the inverse of resistance, the voltage required per unit current.]{.definition-explanation} Reading the conductance can recover a stored weight. Such storage is [[**nonvolatile**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}: it can retain its state without continuous power, within its retention limits.]{.definition-explanation} Nonvolatile weights can remain after the changing neural state has disappeared.
The following choices locate the stored quantity before we compare complete machines.

Here [[**device mismatch**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means persistent differences between nominally identical circuit elements.]{.definition-explanation} It differs from fluctuations that vary from moment to moment. A fixed mismatch can create a repeatable bias. Changing noise can create a different trajectory on each trial. We will measure these separately.

To understand a machine's memory, follow one input through it. On a digital spiking processor, an arriving event identifies connections, their weights contribute to inputs, and a program updates stored neuron variables. Those variables determine whether to send further events. Loihi 2 provides local digital state and weight memory with programmable neuron and learning rules. SpiNNaker2 uses many processor cores whose software updates neural states stored with weights in local SRAM. Their event communication does not make every model variable evolve continuously in physical time.[^hardware-intel][^hardware-spinnaker]

In an analog neural circuit, an input can directly supply current to a capacitor. Transistors implement leakage and other responses as the voltage evolves. Digital circuits may still route the events and store the settings. [[**Mixed-signal hardware**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} combines analog circuit variables with digital storage, communication, or calculation.]{.definition-explanation} The division of labor, rather than the label, determines which dynamics are physical and which are calculated.

PCM supplies a third use of physics. At a fixed, sufficiently small read voltage, a cell's current is approximately $I=GV$, where $I$ is current, $V$ is applied voltage, and $G$ is conductance, measured in siemens (amperes per volt). The stored conductance represents a weight. In Le Gallo and colleagues' chip, the duration of a read pulse represents the input magnitude. For one positive contribution with fixed $G$ and $V$, a pulse lasting $T$ seconds passes charge $Q\simeq GVT$. The contribution is proportional to the product of weight and input duration. Currents from several cells add, and the chip converts the combined current over time to digital values. Signed inputs and weights require additional polarity handling beyond this simple example.[^hardware-legallo]

[[**In-memory computing**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} performs some operations where the values are stored, reducing the need to transfer them to a separate arithmetic unit.]{.definition-explanation} The 64-core PCM chip demonstrates this approach to neural-network inference, with digital processing also part of the system. Its weighted response results from both the stored material state and the applied input signal.

[A circuit's storage medium tells us how a value is retained between updates. Its update rule tells us how that value affects subsequent computation. Both are needed to explain memory.]{.key-statement} We can now examine why feedback can preserve a bit yet let a graded estimate wander.

<!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = NO --> A circuit can remain active for seconds even when its individual voltages decay in milliseconds. The explanation is feedback: activity supplies new input before old input disappears. But long-lived activity does not by itself identify what is being preserved. This chapter first explains how feedback extends a time scale, then distinguishes a restoring discrete memory from a freely changing continuous one. Measured silicon circuits show why this distinction matters beyond a mathematical model. <!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = YES -->

**Physical mechanism.** An isolated capacitor loses a voltage difference when charge leaks through a resistance. In a recurrent circuit, its output can cause an input current that replaces some of that charge. The competition between loss and replacement sets the decay of the collective state. For a neural population, the same competition occurs between decay of synaptic input and input supplied by recurrent spikes.
Let $u$ be the amplitude of one small activity disturbance around a reference state. A simple linear model is

Here $\tau_s$ is the component decay time, $g$ is dimensionless recurrent feedback gain, and $I(t)$ is external drive expressed in the same units as $u$. The term $-u$ removes activity, and $gu$ replaces a fraction of that loss. After the cue ends, $I=0$. For $g<1$,

**Interpretation.** Raising $g$ toward one slows forgetting. At $g=1$, this ideal linear mode retains every amplitude. For $g>1$, it grows until effects omitted from the linear model become important. [Long persistence requires a balance of physical processes. It is not determined by the storage element's decay time alone.]{.key-statement}

<!-- vale ai-tells.ContrastiveFormulas = NO --> With no external input, divide the differential equation by $\tau_s$: $du/dt=-(1-g)u/\tau_s$. Multiplying by $e^{(1-g)t/\tau_s}$ makes the derivative of $u e^{(1-g)t/\tau_s}$ zero. Its value is the initial amplitude $u(0)$. Comparing the resulting exponential with $e^{-t/\tau_{\rm eff}}$ gives the effective time constant above. This is one linear mode near a chosen state, not a full transistor or spiking-network model. <!-- vale ai-tells.ContrastiveFormulas = YES -->
<div class="publisher-worked-calculation publisher-fold-always">
**Example: a small gain error changes a long memory time.**

Choose $\tau_s=10$ ms. Gain $g=0.99$ gives $\tau_{\rm eff}=1$ s. Changing the gain to $0.98$ reduces that time to $0.5$ s. Changing it to $0.995$ increases it to $2$ s. The component decay time is unchanged in these three cases. The example predicts sensitivity to adjusting the feedback strength, not a measured lifetime on any chip.
The next issue is which disturbances the feedback corrects. Retaining any amplitude requires a different response from restoring one chosen amplitude.
<!-- vale ai-tells.StackedAnaphora = NO -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.StackedAnaphora = YES -->

**Physical mechanism.** In a two-state electronic memory, feedback pushes a slightly disturbed state back toward the same stable state. A sufficiently large disturbance can switch it to the other state. In an ideal continuous attractor, disturbances away from the family of memory states decay, but a displacement along that family represents another valid value. The circuit has no restoring signal telling it which earlier value to recover. Seung used this distinction to compare discrete electronic memory with graded eye-position memory.[^dynamics-seung]

<!-- vale ai-tells.ContrastiveFormulas = NO --> This is a distinction between dynamics, not a division between all digital and all analog machines. Analog transistors can maintain discrete bits. Digital processors can calculate a continuous-state neural model to finite precision. Stored bits may remain correct while repeated numerical updates produce a wandering decoded angle. <!-- vale ai-tells.ContrastiveFormulas = YES -->

**Mathematical comparison.** Let $e$ measure a local displacement from one stable state. If restoration has strength $\kappa>0$ and random perturbations have diffusion coefficient $D$, a reduced model is
The Brownian increment $dW_t$ has variance $dt$. Here $\kappa$ has units of inverse time and $D$ has units of $e^2$/time. Starting exactly at the stable state,
For a neutral memory direction with $\kappa=0$, the corresponding result is $\operatorname{Var}(e(t))=2Dt$. Restoration limits small local fluctuations. A neutral direction accumulates them.

<!-- vale ai-tells.FillerPhrases = NO --> The linear stochastic equation has solution $e(t)=\sqrt{2D}\int_0^t e^{-\kappa(t-s)}dW_s$ when $e(0)=0$. Independent Brownian increments make its variance the integral of the squared weighting function: $2D\int_0^t e^{-2\kappa(t-s)}ds=D(1-e^{-2\kappa t})/\kappa$. As $\kappa$ tends to zero, expanding the exponential gives $2Dt$. This is a local model inside one stable state's region of attraction. It does not describe rare switches between digital states or estimate a hardware bit-error rate. <!-- vale ai-tells.FillerPhrases = YES -->

**Interpretation.** Adding restoration to an angle memory can reduce random spread by drawing nearby angles toward preferred positions. That also reduces the set of distinct values retained. [[**Pinning**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that imperfections or imposed structure draw a nominally continuous memory toward preferred states.]{.definition-explanation} A flat error variance can mean successful retention near one preferred value while other cues have been biased toward it. Both mean error and spread are needed.

<!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO --> [Burak and Fiete's diffusion bound concerns a specified noisy neural memory model. It is not a lower bound on the error of every electronic memory.]{.key-statement} A digital device that freezes a number, uses explicit error correction, or changes the noise and readout assumptions poses a different problem. To transfer the bound, match the dynamics, noise, available observations, and time scale first.[^dynamics-burak] <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES -->

A physical demonstration lets us test whether feedback maintains the intended state despite unequal devices and finite resolution. The following early experiments make different claims and should be read separately.

Massoud and Horiuchi built a head-direction circuit whose localized activity could persist after a cue and move with velocity input. It had 32 bump positions around a circle, a spacing of $11.25^\circ$. This demonstrates a physical orientation representation with finite resolution. It does not establish an exact continuum of persistent states or a measured Brownian diffusion law.[^dynamics-massoud]

Giulioni and colleagues built a recurrent spiking circuit with low and high activity states. Brief stimulation could initiate activity lasting seconds despite millisecond circuit dynamics. Their measurements also examined noise-driven transitions and recovery after disturbance. This is [[**bistability**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}: two locally stable states under the same ongoing conditions.]{.definition-explanation} It supplies a physical working-memory example, but its two-state retention is a different task from retaining an arbitrary angle.[^dynamics-giulioni]

The comparison gives a useful reading rule for current machines: determine what values the network distinguishes, then ask how long and how accurately it preserves them. Neuron count or nonvolatile weight storage cannot answer those questions alone.

Suppose we want to study how a noisy network retains an angle. One machine can calculate every state update as arithmetic. Another can let capacitor voltages perform part of the dynamics. A third can use material conductances to multiply inputs by stored weights. The scientific choice is which physical effects we want to control, measure, or exploit. This chapter compares these implementations and then examines recent demonstrations of memory and learning.

<!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO --> The research snapshot is **October 30, 2026**. “State of the art” here means selected recent capabilities supported by primary papers, with older architecture papers supplying their physical explanation. It does not mean one machine leads every task. We distinguish measured chips, experiments partly run on a separate computer, and proposed hardware evaluated by simulation. A [[**host computer**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a separate general-purpose computer that controls an experiment or performs calculations assigned outside the neuromorphic chip.]{.definition-explanation} <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES -->

A useful platform must make the variables of interest accessible. If the question concerns a specific noise law, a digital update may allow precise control of the injected noise. If the question concerns physical circuit variability, analog dynamics expose that variability directly. Interpreting either choice as a biological result requires a matched model and experiment. [[**Hardware calibration**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} adjusts circuit settings to make measured device responses match requested responses more closely.]{.definition-explanation}

The first two rows describe digital neural computation, while BrainScaleS-2 directly implements parts of the differential equations in analog circuitry. Its dynamics run roughly a thousand times faster than the biological model time. That acceleration makes long model intervals accessible quickly, but communication and measurement delays still occur in physical time.[^systems-architecture]

[[**On-chip learning**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that circuitry on the chip computes and applies some weight changes.]{.definition-explanation} It is distinct from loading previously trained weights. Loihi 2 offers programmable learning rules. SpiNNaker2's 2026 technical preprint reports an on-chip learning implementation. BrainScaleS-2 combines local measurements with programmable processors that update weights. An experiment may still use weights trained beforehand or learning performed on a separate computer, so its learning setup must be checked.[^systems-learning]
The following studies make progress on different parts of the memory problem. For each, ask what information persists and which physical component is responsible.

**A useful input history on Loihi 2, 2025.** Kleyko and colleagues implemented a stored history of recent inputs and functions of those inputs that include products. A trained readout uses these values to predict an output. This shows that changing chip state can supply useful information about recent inputs. It is not a measurement of indefinitely stable cue retention. Their pictured Hala Point system is much larger than the resources used in the experiment.[^systems-kleyko]

**Persistent spatial activity on SpiNNaker 2, September 2026.** Aitsam and colleagues ran a 768-neuron recurrent sheet on one chip, with signals from a physical event camera. During an eight-second interval without input, the decoded activity center moved by at most half a cell. The eight seconds establish persistence for that interval, not a measured lifetime. The robot-guidance evaluation used a simulated robot. Its power figures were estimates. The study supplies a current physical implementation on which longer-delay and noise-controlled tests would be useful.[^systems-aitsam]

**Rapid adaptation using PCM, 2025.** Ortner and colleagues used physical PCM weights for a recurrent spiking network that produced robotic-arm commands after a task-specific update. Earlier training adjusted the model for rapid adaptation to new tasks. The PCM units performed matrix-vector products. Other operations ran on a host computer. This locates the demonstrated advance in weight adaptation and mixed hardware computation. It does not show that PCM cells themselves sustained an autonomous recurrent activity pattern.[^systems-ortner]

<!-- vale ai-tells.ContrastiveFormulas = NO --> **Reduced material drift, online 2025 and in a 2026 issue.** Wang and colleagues measured low resistance drift in a chromium-telluride phase-change material, CrTe$_3$. Reduced drift can help a programmed conductance continue representing the intended weight. Their demonstration of several programmed resistance levels used laser programming and electrical readout. Electrical switching was a separate demonstration. Operation with several levels in nanoscale devices, performance beyond a million programming cycles, and variability across large arrays remained open. This is progress in a storage material, not a complete multilevel neuromorphic processor.[^systems-wang] <!-- vale ai-tells.ContrastiveFormulas = YES -->

[Better temporal state, faster adaptation, and more stable weights solve different problems, so progress in one does not establish the others.]{.key-statement} For the Burak comparison, the missing measurement is often how a decoded value changes during an input-free delay.

Fast spiking units can lose earlier inputs before a later decision needs them. One solution is to add a slower state that summarizes recent activity and sends input back to the fast units. Sun and colleagues' 2026 dual-memory-pathway design takes this route. Its proposed digital hardware holds successive slow states in [[**registers**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, small, fast digital storage locations]{.definition-explanation}, and other variables in SRAM. The hardware results came from post-layout simulations, which model a circuit after its physical layout has been designed. They were not measurements of a fabricated chip. The weights were trained before the evaluated tasks.[^systems-sun]
A simple model shows what a slow state buys. Let $z_k$ be current input to a stored quantity $m_k$:

Here $k$ counts updates, $\alpha$ is the retained fraction, and $\beta$ converts input units into state units. After input stops, $m_{k+n}=\alpha^n m_k$. The state remembers earlier input through its present value, while gradually forgetting it. This model illustrates slow storage. It is not the full equations or an independent performance test of Sun and colleagues' architecture.
<div class="publisher-worked-calculation publisher-fold-always">
**Example: the update interval determines the physical memory time.**

If updates are separated by $\Delta t$, equating $\alpha^n$ with $e^{-n\Delta t/\tau_m}$ gives $\tau_m=-\Delta t/\ln\alpha$. With $\Delta t=1$ ms and $\alpha=0.999$, $\tau_m$ is about 1 second. Executing the same updates a thousand times faster reduces that physical decay time to about 1 millisecond, unless the mapping between model time and wall time is changed. A number described as “slow” must be specified relative to other processes and the task clock.

Scaling a network also adds communication constraints. Ilmberger and Schemmel's 2025 preprint measured communication in a four-chip BrainScaleS-2 prototype. The timing matters because its analog states continue changing while messages are transmitted. A small delay in wall time can be a substantial delay in accelerated model time.[^systems-multichip]

The comparison needs a specified task, permitted error, delay, and system boundary. Energy for a matrix operation omits state maintenance, communication, conversion, and host work when those are outside the measured unit. The next chapter turns these qualifications into an experiment that can compare the machines on the same memory question.

<!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO --> After a circuit receives an angle cue, its later estimate may be wrong because the state wandered, because unequal connections pull it toward another angle, or because the observer reads it poorly. One accuracy score combines these causes. The controlled tests below connect these errors to physical parameters. The protocol and reduced models below are proposed tools for reasoning about these experiments, not results already demonstrated on every platform in the previous chapter. <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES -->

Begin with a circuit whose joint activity represents an angle. Choose a decoder on separate calibration data, then keep it fixed while testing retention. A [[**decoder**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a specified rule for estimating the represented quantity from observable circuit signals.]{.definition-explanation} A decoder given every internal state has a different task from a downstream neuron receiving only spikes.
Use the following sequence:
Present a brief cue for angle $\theta_0$, then remove it. Test many angles, including values between any suspected preferred positions.
Hold the connection weights fixed during each retention trial. Record the actual settings, temperature, update interval, and any imposed noise.

Repeat trials at several delays $t$ and decode $\hat\theta(t)$. Use a common reference for angular differences. [[**Unwrapping**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} tracks crossings of $0^\circ/360^\circ$ by adding or subtracting full turns to continue the trajectory.]{.definition-explanation} Use it only when sampling is frequent enough to identify crossings reliably.
Report mean error and error variance separately as functions of cue and delay. Also report failures in which the activity pattern disappears or changes form.
Repeat with changed noise, calibration, or numerical precision, changing one factor at a time. Compare with the same model running in a numerical reference implementation.

Record the decoded state immediately after each cue so that error in writing the value can be separated from error accumulated during retention. Report the number of repeated trials and uncertainty in the estimated drift and diffusion.

[An active circuit has demonstrated useful memory only when its later signals distinguish the earlier cues at the required accuracy.]{.key-statement} High firing rate alone does not establish this. Nor does a small average error if positive and negative errors cancel.
For short intervals, a useful local model is

Here $b(\theta)$ is systematic angular motion per unit time and $D(\theta)$ is half the local variance growth rate. With nearly constant coefficients over a short lag $\Delta t$, repeated trials near the same angle give $\mathbb E[\Delta\theta]\simeq b\Delta t$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\Delta\theta)\simeq2D\Delta t$. Correlated perturbations, preferred states, or boundaries can invalidate that short-lag fit. At long delays, report the distribution of angular errors around the circle. Values separated by a full turn represent the same angle, so a local unwrapped variance cannot be extended indefinitely as a measure of angular error.

Estimate readout noise before interpreting short-lag variance as motion of the stored value. Independent errors with constant variance in two position readings add a constant offset to the measured displacement variance.

Suppose each position estimate contains independent, zero-mean measurement error with variance $\sigma_m^2$. The difference of two estimates then adds $2\sigma_m^2$ to displacement variance, even when the circuit does not move. For independent constant-$D$ state motion, the measured short-lag displacement variance is $2D\Delta t+2\sigma_m^2$. A nonzero intercept can reveal this contribution. Correlated readout errors, overlapping observation windows, or a state that changes during the readout require a fuller model. This is the same type of separation needed when interpreting the eye-drift measurements.

A changed component affects memory through the circuit's equations. Increasing a leak current can shorten a component time constant. Changing a recurrent weight can alter restoration or introduce a preferred angle. A fluctuating current can perturb many neurons, yet only part of the resulting activity change remains as a change of the remembered angle.

The [projection derived in Part I](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-linearization) makes the last statement precise. Let the vector $\mathbf r$ contain the network's activity variables, with local dynamics $d\mathbf r=\mathbf f(\mathbf r)dt+B\,d\mathbf W_t$. The matrix $B$ maps independent Brownian disturbances into those variables. Near a family $\mathbf r_*(\theta)$ of steady states, let $\boldsymbol\ell$ be the left neutral vector, normalized so that $\boldsymbol\ell^T d\mathbf r_*/d\theta=1$. It converts an activity disturbance into its surviving angular displacement. The leading local approximation gives

[Noise matters through both its size and the directions in which it pushes the circuit.]{.key-statement} Large disturbances in rapidly corrected directions can matter less than small disturbances along the memory direction. In a general network the left neutral vector differs from the visible tangent to the family. Using the tangent alone can predict the wrong sensitivity. Curvature and state-dependent noise can also contribute drift beyond this local approximation.

Write $\delta\theta\simeq\boldsymbol\ell^T\delta\mathbf r$ in the local linear regime. For the neutral mode, $\boldsymbol\ell^T$ times the linearized deterministic drift is zero. The stochastic increment is $d\theta\simeq\boldsymbol\ell^TB\,d\mathbf W_t$. Since $\operatorname{Cov}(d\mathbf W_t)=I\,dt$, its variance is $\boldsymbol\ell^TBB^T\boldsymbol\ell\,dt$. Equating this to $2D\,dt$ gives the displayed coefficient. The normalization ensures that the result measures angular displacement rather than an arbitrarily scaled activity coordinate. This calculation transfers only after the hardware's local dynamics and noise assumptions have been checked.
The following changes suggest tests under the model assumptions above.
<div class="publisher-worked-calculation publisher-fold-always">
**Example: a tighter distribution can hide a biased memory.**

Consider two illustrative circuits after a one-second delay. Circuit A has zero mean angular error and variance $4$ deg$^2$. Circuit B has mean error $3^\circ$ and variance $1$ deg$^2$, because it is attracted toward a preferred angle. Their mean squared errors are $4$ and $1+3^2=10$ deg$^2$. Circuit B has less random spread but worse cue retention. Reporting only its smaller variance would hide the effect of pinning.
The source papers supply different constraints on this hardware experiment.

**Burak and Fiete (2012):** compare diffusion with the information available in spikes under matched noise, dynamics, and observation assumptions. A processor that stores an exact internal angle and exposes it directly to the decoder has changed the readout problem.

**Ben-Shushan and colleagues (2022):** a measured output can filter the internal command. Camera exposure, output smoothing, or a mechanical actuator can change the observed motion. Calibrate that path before assigning an output time scale to the memory circuit itself.
<!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = NO -->

**Mainali and colleagues (2025):** patterns of firing across physical positions constrain a spatial representation. Reproducing field-size statistics does not by itself show that a network implemented in hardware retains position without input. Spatial structure and temporal persistence need separate tests.
<!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = YES -->

These links concern the tested mechanisms, not a claim that a chip reproduces the animal systems. The [synthesis chapter](ch-synthesis.html#sec-synthesis-evidence) sets out the evidence supplied by the original papers.

Time conversion is especially important for accelerated hardware. If model time $t_m=a t_p$, where $t_p$ is physical time and $a>1$ is the acceleration factor, a diffusion law $\operatorname{Var}(\Delta\theta)=2D_m t_m$ becomes $2(aD_m)t_p$. The result is $D_p=aD_m$ when expressed per physical second. This is a change of units for the same ideal trajectory. Physical communication delay, temperature drift, or limited readout speed can prevent a real device from obeying that ideal rescaling.

For an energy comparison, specify the cue distribution, delay, permitted decoding error, and failed-trial rate. Measure energy over writing, waiting, and reading, including required host processing and interfaces. Then report how error and energy change as delay increases. An operations-per-second or operations-per-watt figure alone cannot establish the cost of retaining a useful value.

The resulting research question is concrete: **which part of the physical implementation limits the accuracy of a remembered quantity, and does changing that part improve retention under the same task and readout?** That question turns von Neumann's comparison into a test of contemporary neural and electronic memory mechanisms.
